cim: Who wants a lamp that wants to be wanted?
cim_eredeti: Who wants a lamp that wants to be wanted?
szoveg_eredeti:
In the 2004 comedy Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy, the dim-witted Brick Tamland (played by Steve Carell) blurts, “I love lamp!”

In 2004, it was a joke. Now it’s a business plan.

A burgeoning industry is working hard to make us all “love lamp.” But how do you make a lamp lovable?

In February of last year, I told you about an Apple research project, and the paper it produced, aimed at giving a lamp a personality. Created by Apple’s Machine Learning Research division, the ELEGNT project used AI to give a non-humanoid desktop robot the expressiveness of a person or a pet.

In other words, Apple built something with the body of a lamp and the body language of a pet.

The robot lamp was designed to “pay attention” to the user’s actions and words, and respond like it understood. The lamp could speak, but its signature trick was body language: nodding, shaking, and tilting its “head,” wagging a figurative “tail” with its arm, and leaning forward and “gazing” to simulate interest and attention. Open a book, and the lamp turned to face it, lit the page, and “read” along, adding related information with a projector.

The ELEGNT project, which drew on Pixar’s 1986 short Luxo Jr., helped spark today’s fascination with lamps that have personalities, even though Apple shows no sign of wanting to sell a lovable lamp. Its approach of expressive movement resembles what’s been reported about Apple’s desktop robot, code-named J595.

The unannounced, unnamed product is a tabletop robot that can control smart-home devices and has a 9-inch screen mounted on a motorized arm. It’s basically an iPad attached to a robot arm that moves and tilts for both personality and practicality, such as keeping the screen trained on you during a FaceTime call no matter where you move. Apple’s desktop robot is expected to cost about $1,000 and come out in 2027 or 2028.

The attachment economy is an emerging business model that takes the attention economy even further.

In the attention economy, human attention is treated as a scarce resource (because there’s so much information and entertainment available to everyone), and companies, especially ad-funded ones, compete to capture it as a core part of their business models. Social media companies, for example, tweak their algorithms to prioritize whatever leaves us furious, fractious, or flushed.

The attachment economy grabs attention by using AI to simulate human or animal attributes in order to encourage users to form emotional attachments to AI products, essentially hijacking the natural human capacity to form loving bonds with people or pets and redirecting it at a product. Relationship bots, robot pets, and humanoid robots are obvious examples.

The attention economy wanted our eyes. The attachment economy wants our hearts.

Reports say J595’s hardware has been largely finished for about two years while Apple keeps working out the software. My own speculation is that Apple may not be sure whether it wants to join the attachment economy with a lovable desktop robot (just as it has kept its devices mostly free of the attention economy’s ad-driven design) or just keep it functional.

Apple isn’t planning a lovable lamp. But other companies are.

A company called Autonomous, which made its name selling standing desks and office chairs and now also sells AI hardware, makes a lamp creatively named… Lamp. The $699 “personal robot” moves, sees, and hears, and it runs Claude Code, Codex, and Hermes. It ships December 19, according to the website.

Lamp has servos for movement, a wide-angle camera with face tracking and motion sensing, a microphone array, and stereo speakers. The company claims Lamp comes with 70 skills (which is 69 more than a regular lamp). Users can talk to the lamp, show it things, and have it respond to what it sees and hears with speech and movement. It runs on the company’s hosted AI by default. Owners can connect their own agent or AI account instead, but voice, face recognition, and mood features still rely on Autonomous’ service.

In various marketing content, the company says that Lamp is a “living” personal computer that “thinks.”

When I challenged them on this, a company representative told me that the “living” and “thinks” claims are “product language about an interactive AI-powered device, not… a claim that Lamp is alive or conscious.”

The company is familiar with the idea of the attachment economy. It claims their goal “isn’t to make people emotionally dependent on a robot,” but to “make the interaction more natural.”

“We want people to enjoy interacting with Lamp because it’s useful and expressive, not because they feel emotionally dependent on it.”

I suspect this will be a commonly expressed claim by companies in the emerging attachment economy: “No, we’re not trying to encourage emotional attachment as part of the business model, we just want customers to love it.”

Another personality lamp on the market is called Mori, from the Singapore-based company OKA. The robot is programmed to act “curious, shy, and sometimes playful.” It doesn’t speak, and instead expresses simulated emotions and reactions through movement, light, sound, and eye expressions.

It’s designed to be a somewhat passive and background robot, making eye expressions timed with sounds for an effect on users. It blinks, looks around, and responds to physical touch. The robot even stares at you when you’re not paying attention to it and is designed to “act shy” around strangers.

The Mori robot is shaped like a mushroom, and when it becomes active, the top rises and eyes peer out from under the lid. Expression comes from lights, tilting of the “head,” and eye movement.

Marketing videos show the lamp “inviting you to nature,” asking you to touch it while it plays nature soundscapes such as rainfall, and swaying along to music when people dance in their seats.

Ambitiously, OKA claims that people are “increasingly disconnected from themselves and what makes them human” and says it is exploring how AI and robotics can reverse that trend.

To put it bluntly, Mori is designed to give users who lack nature and relationships in their lives an ersatz version of both.

OKA says the lamp robot has “VIBE,” which stands for Vitality, Interaction, Bonding, and Emotion, an internal state that changes over time.

OKA claims “Mori is alive.” The company also says Mori has an inner state, emotion, mood, curiosity, shyness, hope, and an “appetite for company.”

OKA didn’t respond to my request for comment.

AI can make a lamp lovable and give it personality, but there’s another company lighting the way to a different AI lamp future.

The Syncere Lume is an AI floor lamp with no personality whatsoever. It’s a home robot that goes to extreme lengths to exhibit zero humanoid or creature attributes.

The $2,699 lamp sits in the corner providing light. But it can also get to work, moving to another place in the house and using its robot arm to make the bed, fold laundry, load the dishwasher, and tidy up. By wearing a “Personalization Band,” you can show the robot how to do your chores, and it copies your actions, according to the company.

The company hopes to start shipping the Lume in the first half of next year to invited customers in New York and the San Francisco Bay Area, followed by everyone else later, presumably.

These products raise interesting questions about the future of home and desktop robots. First, does the public want robot lamps? And, if so, what do people want their robot lamps to do? Be a friend? Make the bed? Or something else?

Robots in the home feel inevitable. And so does the attachment economy.

What we don’t know is whether robot lamps are a bright idea or a dim one.

Brick Tamland “loved lamp.” But will anyone else?

Mike Elgan is a technology journalist, author, and podcaster who explores the intersection of advanced technologies and culture through his Computerworld column, Machine Society newsletter, Superintelligent pod
